objective: Mercantilism (16th-17th century) advocates maintaining trade surplus by encouraging exports and restricting imports, viewing trade as a zero-sum game.；Absolute Advantage theory (Adam Smith, 1776) proposes that countries specialize in products they produce more efficiently than others, overturning the zero-sum assumption to make trade positive-sum.；Heckscher-Ohlin theory links comparative advantage to national factor endowments (land, labor, capital); more abundant factors lead to lower production costs and stronger export competitiveness.

learningGoals.statement: Explain mercantilism as a zero-sum trade policy and distinguish it from later positive-sum trade theories.
Distinguish absolute advantage from comparative advantage and explain how specialization improves total output.
Explain how factor endowments shape comparative advantage under the Heckscher-Ohlin theory.
Compare product life cycle theory and new trade theory as complementary explanations of international trade.
Apply international trade theories to justify business location decisions and trade policy stances.

questions.stem: According to mercantilism, if Country X runs a trade surplus with Country Y, what is the most accurate description of Country Y's position?
questions.successCriteria: Student identifies that mercantilism views trade as zero-sum, so one country's surplus is another's loss.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of key aspects of trade theories and explain how they are reflected in international trading practices.
questions.alignmentNote: Directly assesses mercantilism, a core trade theory under EE1.1.
questions.stemIntent: Checks whether students recognize mercantilism's zero-sum assumption.
questions.commonMisconception: Student assumes trade can make both countries better off, importing a positive-sum idea into mercantilism.

options.label: A
options.text: Country Y loses because mercantilism views trade as zero-sum.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Mercantilism treats trade as a zero-sum game: one country's surplus is another's loss.

options.label: B
options.text: Country Y also gains because both countries enjoy the same benefits from trade.
options.feedbackWrong: That is the positive-sum view of later trade theories, not mercantilism. Mercantilism assumes one country's surplus is another's loss.

options.label: C
options.text: Country Y is unaffected because mercantilism only focuses on exports.
options.feedbackWrong: Mercantilism depends on trade balances; a surplus for X implies a deficit for Y, which mercantilists viewed as a loss.

options.label: D
options.text: Country Y gains as long as the goods are cheaper than domestic production.
options.feedbackWrong: That reasoning reflects comparative advantage logic, not mercantilism.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes absolute advantage from comparative advantage?
questions.successCriteria: Student explains absolute advantage as output per unit of input and comparative advantage as lower opportunity cost.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of key aspects of trade theories and explain how they are reflected in international trading practices.
questions.alignmentNote: Distinguishing absolute and comparative advantage is a key aspect of trade theory under EE1.1.
questions.stemIntent: Checks whether students can separate efficiency-based absolute advantage from opportunity-cost-based comparative advantage.
questions.commonMisconception: Student equates absolute advantage with lower opportunity cost, mixing the two concepts.

options.label: A
options.text: Absolute advantage compares how much a country can produce with the same resources; comparative advantage compares opportunity cost.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Absolute advantage is about productive efficiency; comparative advantage is about lower opportunity cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Absolute advantage compares opportunity cost; comparative advantage compares output per worker.
options.feedbackWrong: That is backwards. Absolute advantage is about efficiency measured by output per input; comparative advantage is about lower opportunity cost.

options.label: C
options.text: Absolute advantage determines exports; comparative advantage determines imports.
options.feedbackWrong: Both concepts can determine trade patterns; the distinction is in how advantage is measured, not which side of the border it applies to.

options.label: D
options.text: The two concepts are interchangeable and state the same idea.
options.feedbackWrong: They are related but distinct: a country can have absolute advantage in all goods yet still gain from specializing according to comparative advantage.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks a non-zero-sum option on the mercantilism question or gives an incorrect open response showing trade as positive-sum for all.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student treats mercantilism as a positive-sum theory, importing later trade theory logic into a 16th-17th century zero-sum framework.

miniLesson.explain: Mercantilism (16th-17th century) is a trade theory that advocates maintaining a trade surplus by encouraging exports and restricting imports. It views trade as a zero-sum game: one country's surplus must be another country's loss. If Country X runs a surplus with Country Y, X's gain is Y's loss. This contrasts with Adam Smith's 1776 absolute advantage theory, which shows specialization and trade can be positive-sum and raise overall output and living standards.
miniLesson.example: In the lesson's simplified two-country, two-product example, mercantilists would applaud a country that exports more than it imports, but they would see the trading partner's deficit as a loss. Under Adam Smith's 1776 view, both countries can gain by specializing in what they produce more efficiently, making trade positive-sum rather than zero-sum.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Zero-sum means one country's surplus is another's loss—mercantilism sees trade as a win-lose contest, not a win-win exchange.

guidedPractice.prompt: What does 'zero-sum' mean in mercantilism? If Country X has a trade surplus with Country Y, what is Country Y's position according to mercantilism?
guidedPractice.answer: Zero-sum means one country's gain is exactly balanced by another country's loss. In mercantilism, if Country X has a trade surplus, Country Y has a trade deficit and is seen as losing; X's surplus is Y's loss.

guidedPractice.prompt: A country following mercantilist policy encourages exports and restricts imports. Explain how this creates a zero-sum outcome for its trading partner.
guidedPractice.answer: By encouraging exports, the country earns revenue from abroad; by restricting imports, it reduces spending on foreign goods. The resulting trade surplus is matched by the partner's trade deficit, so mercantilism sees the surplus country's gain as the deficit country's loss—total wealth does not increase.

guidedPractice.prompt: Compare mercantilism's zero-sum view with Adam Smith's 1776 absolute advantage theory. Why did Smith's theory overturn the zero-sum assumption?
guidedPractice.answer: Mercantilism treats trade as a fixed pie: a surplus for one country is a loss for another. Adam Smith's 1776 absolute advantage theory argues that countries specialize in goods they produce more efficiently, increasing total output and making both trading partners better off. This makes trade positive-sum, not zero-sum.

reteachModules.trigger: Student confuses efficiency-based absolute advantage with opportunity-cost-based comparative advantage on the relevant questions.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student thinks absolute advantage means having the lower opportunity cost, or believes the two concepts are interchangeable. They may not realize that a country with absolute advantage in all goods can still benefit from specialization according to comparative advantage.

miniLesson.explain: Absolute advantage, from Adam Smith's 1776 theory, means a country can produce a good more efficiently than another country—using the same resources to produce more output. Comparative advantage means a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost, meaning it gives up less of another good to make it. These are different ideas: a country can have absolute advantage in every good, but it cannot have comparative advantage in every good. According to Heckscher-Ohlin theory, comparative advantage originates from differences in national factor endowments like land, labor, and capital. Specialization and trade improve overall output and raise living standards, as demonstrated by simple two-country, two-product models.
miniLesson.example: In the simplified two-country, two-product example used in class, one country may be more efficient at producing both goods. Yet both countries still gain if each specializes in the good where it has the lower opportunity cost. The key is not who produces more, but who gives up less to produce it.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Absolute = Able (efficiency, output per input). Comparative = Cost (opportunity cost). If you confuse them, remember: 'A is for Able, C is for Cost.'

guidedPractice.prompt: Define absolute advantage and comparative advantage in one sentence each.
guidedPractice.answer: Absolute advantage is producing a good more efficiently than another country (higher output with the same resources). Comparative advantage is producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country.

guidedPractice.prompt: In the simplified two-country, two-product model, Country Alpha can produce both wheat and cloth more efficiently than Country Beta. Explain why Alpha and Beta can still both gain from trade.
guidedPractice.answer: Even though Alpha has absolute advantage in both goods, trade can still benefit both if each country specializes in the good for which it has a lower opportunity cost—that is, its comparative advantage. Specialization and trade increase total output, so both countries can be better off.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student says: 'Since Country A can produce everything more efficiently than Country B, Country B should just buy everything from A.' Identify the error and state the correct specialization rule.
guidedPractice.answer: The error is confusing absolute advantage with comparative advantage. Even if Country A produces everything more efficiently, Country B can still have a lower opportunity cost in one good. Both countries gain more by specializing according to comparative advantage and trading, rather than Country B buying everything from A.

reteachModules.trigger: Student attributes Heckscher-Ohlin predictions to absolute advantage or ignores factor endowments as the source of comparative advantage.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student thinks Heckscher-Ohlin simply means a country with abundant factors becomes absolutely more efficient at producing everything using those factors, rather than recognizing that factor endowments create comparative advantage through lower opportunity cost.

miniLesson.explain: Heckscher-Ohlin theory links comparative advantage to national factor endowments (land, labor, capital). More abundant factors lead to lower production costs and stronger export competitiveness. This is not about being the absolute best or most efficient producer in every use of that factor. It is about opportunity cost: a country with abundant labor can produce labor-intensive goods at lower opportunity cost, so it specializes in and exports those goods, even if another country is technically more efficient overall. Adam Smith's absolute advantage is about output per input; Heckscher-Ohlin is about factor-based comparative advantage.
miniLesson.example: In a simplified two-country, two-product model, suppose one country has abundant labor and the other has abundant capital. The labor-abundant country will export the labor-intensive good, and the capital-abundant country will export the capital-intensive good, even if the labor-abundant country could also produce the capital-intensive good with slightly fewer resources than its partner. The reason is that the opportunity cost of shifting resources is lower for the country with the abundant factor.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Factor endowments shape comparative advantage, not just 'who is best at everything.' Abundant factor inputs = lower-cost exports. Think opportunity cost, not superiority.

guidedPractice.prompt: According to Heckscher-Ohlin theory, what do differences in national factor endowments (land, labor, capital) determine?
guidedPractice.answer: They determine comparative advantage: a country exports goods that intensively use its more abundant factors because abundance lowers production costs.

guidedPractice.prompt: Country A has abundant capital but less labor than Country B. Country B has abundant labor. If capital-intensive goods are made with many machines, which country is most likely to export capital-intensive goods under Heckscher-Ohlin, and why?
guidedPractice.answer: Country A, because its abundant capital makes capital-intensive production cheaper; this is a comparative advantage from factor abundance, not necessarily absolute advantage.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student argues: 'Heckscher-Ohlin just means that a country with abundant land should be absolutely better at producing everything that uses land.' Explain the flaw using what you know about absolute vs comparative advantage.
guidedPractice.answer: The flaw is confusing absolute advantage with comparative advantage. Heckscher-Ohlin predicts that abundant land lowers the opportunity cost of land-intensive goods, so a land-abundant country specializes in and exports them, but it does not claim that country is absolutely most efficient in all land-using products. Even if another country can produce each good with fewer total inputs, mutually beneficial trade still arises from comparative advantage.

reteachModules.trigger: Diagnostic evidence: student selects or explains that product life cycle theory and new trade theory are mutually exclusive, or that one of these theories alone fully explains modern international trade patterns.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student treats product life cycle theory and new trade theory as competing explanations and assumes modern trade has a single cause, when each theory explains different aspects of trade and they are complementary.

miniLesson.explain: Vernon's product life cycle theory explains trade patterns by following products from newness to maturity: as a product matures, production tends to move to locations that can produce it most efficiently. New trade theory, developed in the 1970s, focuses on economies of scale, which can create first-mover advantages and trade even between countries with similar factor endowments. The two theories are not mutually exclusive. Product life cycle helps explain where production is located at different maturity stages; new trade theory helps explain why early movers in emerging industries dominate and why scale matters. In practice, businesses use both: they disperse production to efficient countries as products mature and invest in first-mover advantages in emerging industries. Therefore, modern trade patterns cannot be reduced to a single cause.
miniLesson.example: A product may first be produced in an innovative country, then shift to a lower-cost country as it matures (product life cycle). Meanwhile, in a new industry, a firm that achieves large scale early gains a lasting cost advantage (new trade theory). Both processes can be observed in the same market, so the two theories complement each other.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: One shows the product's journey as it grows up; the other shows why the first big producer keeps winning. Put them together for the full picture.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which theory from the 1970s focuses on economies of scale?
guidedPractice.answer: New trade theory, developed in the 1970s, emphasizes economies of scale.

guidedPractice.prompt: A mature product is now being produced at the lowest-cost location, while an emerging industry is dominated by a firm that entered early. Which two theories are simultaneously useful here?
guidedPractice.answer: The mature product's location is best explained by Vernon's product life cycle theory; the dominant firm in the emerging industry is best explained by new trade theory's first-mover advantage and economies of scale. They are complementary, not competing.

guidedPractice.prompt: Evaluate this statement: 'Vernon's product life cycle theory explains all modern trade patterns, so new trade theory is unnecessary.' Use the fact bank to explain why the statement is incorrect.
guidedPractice.answer: The statement is incorrect. Product life cycle theory explains trade patterns from product maturity and location of production; new trade theory (1970s) explains economies of scale and first-mover advantages, which the product life cycle does not address. They are complementary: product maturity explains when production moves, while scale and first-mover status explain why many countries with similar factor endowments still trade. Modern trade patterns require both explanations, along with other trade theories.

questions.stem: In the 1600s, Country A follows mercantilist policies: it taxes imports and gives subsidies to exporters, making its trade balance with Country B positive. According to mercantilism, what is the most accurate description of Country B's situation?
options: Country B also gains because trade increases total wealth in both countries.
Country B loses because Country A's surplus is exactly Country B's deficit, and the total wealth is unchanged.
Country B's loss is smaller than Country A's gain, so the world still becomes richer overall.
Country B will automatically specialize in its comparative advantage and catch up.

questions.stem: A modern economist claims: 'The 17th-century mercantilists were right that one country's trade surplus is another country's loss, so free trade only helps one side.' In 2-3 sentences, explain why this statement is incorrect, using Adam Smith's 1776 absolute advantage theory and the lesson's two-country, two-product example.
questions.rubric: Student must state that mercantilism treats trade as a zero-sum game (one country's gain is another's loss), but Adam Smith's absolute advantage theory shows that specialization and trade increase total output, so trade is positive-sum and both countries can gain. The response should use or clearly reference the two-country example (e.g., each country specializes in the product it produces more efficiently).

retestCards.passRule: The student must select the correct single-choice answer (index 1) and the open-ended response must correctly define zero-sum as one country's gain being another's loss and explain that absolute advantage/specialization makes trade positive-sum, with reference to the two-country example.

questions.stem: Two countries, Landia and Seaia, produce fish and grain. Landia can produce each good with fewer resources than Seaia. Which statement correctly describes why both countries can still benefit from specialization and trade?
options: Because Landia should export both goods to Seaia and import nothing.
Because each country should specialize in the good it can produce at a lower opportunity cost, even if Landia is more efficient in both.
Because Seaia has a comparative advantage in both goods since it is less efficient.
Because Landia's absolute advantage in both goods makes trade unnecessary.

questions.stem: In Country A, one worker can produce either 10 tons of rice or 5 tons of corn in a day. In Country B, one worker can produce either 8 tons of rice or 2 tons of corn in a day. Calculate the opportunity cost of producing one ton of corn in each country, then state which country should specialize in corn according to comparative advantage and why.
questions.rubric: Student correctly calculates the opportunity costs: Country A gives up 2 tons of rice for 1 ton of corn (10/5), and Country B gives up 4 tons of rice for 1 ton of corn (8/2). Student identifies that Country A has the lower opportunity cost for corn and should therefore specialize in corn. Student explains that comparative advantage is determined by lower opportunity cost, not by absolute efficiency, and may note that both countries can gain from specialization and trade.

retestCards.passRule: The student must select the correct multiple-choice answer (index 1) and, in the open-ended response, must correctly calculate opportunity costs, identify Country A as the corn specialist based on lower opportunity cost, and clearly distinguish comparative advantage from absolute advantage.

questions.stem: Malaysia has abundant labor but is less productive per worker than Japan in every industry. Japan has abundant capital and is more productive than Malaysia in every industry. According to Heckscher-Ohlin theory, which trade pattern is most likely?
options: Japan should export labor-intensive goods because it is more efficient overall.
Malaysia should export labor-intensive goods because its abundant labor gives it a comparative advantage in those goods.
Malaysia should not trade because Japan is better at everything.
Both countries should produce the same goods to avoid specialization risks.

questions.stem: Using a concrete example (real or created), explain why Heckscher-Ohlin theory predicts trade based on comparative advantage from factor abundance, not on absolute advantage in production. Your answer should clearly distinguish the two concepts.
questions.rubric: Student must (1) state that factor abundance creates comparative advantage through lower opportunity cost, (2) explicitly say that a country need not be absolutely more efficient in the good it exports, and (3) provide a concrete example (e.g., a labor-abundant country exporting textiles despite lower productivity overall, or a capital-abundant country exporting machinery). Full credit requires all three elements.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be correct. The open-ended response must meet the rubric: identify factor endowments as the source of comparative advantage and explicitly distinguish from absolute advantage.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between Vernon's product life cycle theory and new trade theory (1970s)?
options: They are mutually exclusive; only one can apply to any given industry.
They explain different aspects of trade and are complementary.
New trade theory is only useful when product life cycle theory fails.
Product life cycle theory is a specific example of new trade theory.

questions.stem: Use a new example (not from the lesson) to explain how both Vernon's product life cycle theory and new trade theory are needed to understand a modern trade pattern. In your answer, clearly state what each theory contributes.
questions.rubric: A strong answer provides a plausible example (e.g., smartphones, electric vehicles, or a similar product) and explains that the product life cycle theory accounts for production moving from an innovator country to lower-cost countries as the product matures, while new trade theory accounts for early large-scale entrants gaining a lasting cost advantage through economies of scale. The answer must explicitly state that the two theories are complementary, not competing. Award full credit if both theories are correctly identified and applied to the example; partial credit if only one theory is applied or the complementary relationship is not mentioned.

retestCards.passRule: Pass if Q1 is answered correctly (complementary) and Q2 earns at least 2 out of 3 rubric points (i.e., mentions both theories and states they are complementary).

cards.question: According to mercantilism, if Country X runs a trade surplus with Country Y, what is the most accurate description of Country Y's position?
options: Country Y loses because mercantilism views trade as zero-sum.
Country Y also gains because both countries enjoy the same benefits from trade.
Country Y is unaffected because mercantilism only focuses on exports.
Country Y gains as long as the goods are cheaper than domestic production.
cards.diagnosis: Checks whether students recognize mercantilism's zero-sum assumption.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. Mercantilism treats trade as a zero-sum game: one country's surplus is another's loss.
That is the positive-sum view of later trade theories, not mercantilism. Mercantilism assumes one country's surplus is another's loss.
Mercantilism depends on trade balances; a surplus for X implies a deficit for Y, which mercantilists viewed as a loss.
That reasoning reflects comparative advantage logic, not mercantilism.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies that mercantilism views trade as zero-sum, so one country's surplus is another's loss.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of key aspects of trade theories and explain how they are reflected in international trading practices.
cards.alignmentNote: Directly assesses mercantilism, a core trade theory under EE1.1.
cards.commonMisconception: Student assumes trade can make both countries better off, importing a positive-sum idea into mercantilism.

cards.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes absolute advantage from comparative advantage?
options: Absolute advantage compares how much a country can produce with the same resources; comparative advantage compares opportunity cost.
Absolute advantage compares opportunity cost; comparative advantage compares output per worker.
Absolute advantage determines exports; comparative advantage determines imports.
The two concepts are interchangeable and state the same idea.
cards.diagnosis: Checks whether students can separate efficiency-based absolute advantage from opportunity-cost-based comparative advantage.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. Absolute advantage is about productive efficiency; comparative advantage is about lower opportunity cost.
That is backwards. Absolute advantage is about efficiency measured by output per input; comparative advantage is about lower opportunity cost.
Both concepts can determine trade patterns; the distinction is in how advantage is measured, not which side of the border it applies to.
They are related but distinct: a country can have absolute advantage in all goods yet still gain from specializing according to comparative advantage.
cards.successCriteria: Student explains absolute advantage as output per unit of input and comparative advantage as lower opportunity cost.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of key aspects of trade theories and explain how they are reflected in international trading practices.
cards.alignmentNote: Distinguishing absolute and comparative advantage is a key aspect of trade theory under EE1.1.
cards.commonMisconception: Student equates absolute advantage with lower opportunity cost, mixing the two concepts.
